confidence_note: Carr own reading drift and the Friedman line are from notes and essay summaries, not book text. Old diary and Tolstoy invented details dropped; War and Peace is Friedman, not Carr. Plasticity examples from notes. The story presents the thesis as Carr argument, not proof.
facts: The Shallows grew out of Carr 2008 Atlantic essay "Is Google Making Us Stupid?".
Carr writes that for some years he has felt that someone or something has been tinkering with his brain. His concentration drifts after a page or two where he once immersed himself in long prose.
He quotes Bruce Friedman, a blogger on computers in medicine, who says he has almost totally lost the ability to read and absorb a longer text: he cannot read War and Peace anymore.
Carr argues the brain is plastic: it adapts to what it is repeatedly asked to do. Examples: monkeys using tools, violinists, London taxi drivers who build detailed mental maps.
Carr cites research suggesting linear text beats hypertext for comprehension and retention.
scene_details: concentration drifting after a page or two
the mental maps of London taxi drivers
tension: A writer who spent his life reading finds his attention slipping after a page or two.
opening_idea: Start with Carr noticing the page two of a text and his mind leaving.

lessons.idea: The brain strengthens what you ask it to do often, so the way you read now shapes the reader you become.
lessons.anchor: Carr concentration drift and the taxi drivers plasticity.
lessons.example: A cook who only tastes quickly loses patience for slow sauces.

reflect_final: Where in your day is there one stretch of reading or work you could hold in a single piece, and what usually breaks it?

use_cases.situation: You are at your desk and keep switching tabs.
use_cases.move: Say you read how the brain tunes itself to what you repeat, and keep one tab open for 25 minutes.

use_cases.situation: Friends joke that nobody finishes books now.
use_cases.move: Mention Friedman saying he could no longer read War and Peace, and ask what each of you actually finishes.

use_cases.situation: Your family is on phones at dinner.
use_cases.move: Suggest one meal with phones in another room, and notice how the conversation runs.

pocket_idea: The brain gets better at what you repeat, including skimming; pick which one you practise today.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Nicholas Carr says it felt like someone was tinkering with his brain: a page or two and his mind drifted.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Nicholas Carr noticed his concentration drifting after a page or two. A blogger he quotes said he could no longer read War and Peace. Carr argues that the brain adapts to what we repeat, as London taxi drivers show.
